conceptRegistry.label: Boundary
conceptRegistry.definition: A declared distinction that conditions what may cross, transform, or remain separate.

conceptRegistry.label: Interface
conceptRegistry.definition: A typed crossing whose permitted inputs, meanings, actions, and failures are declared.

conceptRegistry.label: Admissibility
conceptRegistry.definition: The conditions under which an operation, transition, or comparison is permitted.

conceptRegistry.label: Defect
conceptRegistry.definition: A typed failure of preservation, correspondence, closure, or lawful transition.

conceptRegistry.label: Closure
conceptRegistry.definition: Completion sufficient for a declared purpose under declared conditions and reopening rules.

conceptRegistry.label: Invariant
conceptRegistry.definition: A structure or relation required to remain preserved under admitted transformation.

conceptRegistry.label: Scope
conceptRegistry.definition: The declared operating domain within which a claim, test, or closure condition applies.

conceptRegistry.label: Reopening
conceptRegistry.definition: A declared condition that lawfully returns closed work to active inquiry or repair.

conceptRegistry.label: Representation
conceptRegistry.definition: A purpose-typed presentation of selected structure from a richer source or carrier.

conceptRegistry.label: Projection
conceptRegistry.definition: A mapping that preserves selected structure while intentionally or consequentially discarding other structure.

conceptRegistry.label: Transport
conceptRegistry.definition: Movement of structure, meaning, or state between declared carriers or contextures.

conceptRegistry.label: Ownership
conceptRegistry.definition: Accountability for maintaining, testing, authorizing, or repairing a bounded object or transition.

conceptRegistry.label: Repair
conceptRegistry.definition: A governed change that restores a failed invariant, correspondence, or reachable path.

conceptRegistry.label: Gauge
conceptRegistry.definition: A declared observational or representational frame that conditions what can be measured or compared.

conceptRegistry.label: Measurement
conceptRegistry.definition: Disciplined representation through a declared instrument, gauge, unit, and precision.

conceptRegistry.label: Trace
conceptRegistry.definition: A preserved record of an operation, observation, transition, or failure.

conceptRegistry.label: Correspondence
conceptRegistry.definition: A declared relation used to compare expected, represented, and observed states.

conceptRegistry.label: Agency
conceptRegistry.definition: The consequential actions an actor can actually reach within declared constraints.

conceptRegistry.label: Standing
conceptRegistry.definition: Recognized authority to enter a process, raise a claim, or seek review and remedy.

conceptRegistry.label: Contestability
conceptRegistry.definition: A reachable and consequential path for challenging a decision, claim, or status.

conceptRegistry.label: Authority
conceptRegistry.definition: Permission to take bounded actions for a declared purpose under reviewable conditions.

conceptRegistry.label: Provenance
conceptRegistry.definition: Durable evidence of origin, transformation, stewardship, and promotion history.

conceptRegistry.label: Transformation
conceptRegistry.definition: A typed operation that changes a carrier or representation under declared rules.

conceptRegistry.label: Identity
conceptRegistry.definition: The structure sufficient to recognize continuity across admitted change.

conceptRegistry.label: Scale
conceptRegistry.definition: A regime of extent or relation that conditions which structure remains accessible.

conceptRegistry.label: Resolution
conceptRegistry.definition: The discriminating capacity of a representation or observational regime.

conceptRegistry.label: Observability
conceptRegistry.definition: Whether a feature can be exposed under declared conditions, instruments, and resolution.

conceptRegistry.label: Purpose
conceptRegistry.definition: The declared end that bounds relevance, sufficiency, and closure.

conceptRegistry.label: On-ramp
conceptRegistry.definition: A familiar example that orients a learner toward formal structure without claiming to establish it.

conceptRegistry.label: Typing
conceptRegistry.definition: Explicit declaration of the kind, domain, and permitted operations of an object or relation.

conceptRegistry.label: Claim ceiling
conceptRegistry.definition: The strongest class of conclusion an artifact is permitted to support.

conceptRegistry.label: Formalization
conceptRegistry.definition: Translation from an intuitive handle into declared objects, relations, operations, and constraints.

onramps.label: Systems & software
onramps.description: Start where an interface turns local success into system failure.

choices.title: The interface kept its syntax and broke its promise.
choices.scene: Two services exchanged valid messages. The workflow still failed because each side meant something different by ‘complete.’
choices.lesson: An interface is more than a connection point. It declares what may cross, what must remain true, and what each side may rely on.
choices.structuralMove: Inspect the contract at the crossing: inputs, meanings, authority, failure behavior, and the invariant the exchange was meant to preserve.
choices.metaphorFirewall: An API illustrates a typed boundary; it does not prove that every social or physical boundary behaves like software.
choices.formalBridge: Describe the two carriers, the admissible transformation between them, and the first condition that fails after transport.

choices.title: Everything was checked off. The work was not actually closed.
choices.scene: The release passed its list, shipped on time, and created a consequence no item on the list was capable of seeing.
choices.lesson: A checklist does not certify universal completeness. It certifies a declared purpose under a declared set of conditions.
choices.structuralMove: Ask what the closure test covered, which consequence sat outside its boundary, and what evidence should lawfully reopen the work.
choices.metaphorFirewall: A checklist is a handle for purpose-bounded closure, not a guarantee that a finite list can capture every possible consequence.
choices.formalBridge: Write the closure predicate, its operating domain, and an explicit reopening condition before adding another task.

onramps.label: Building & engineering
onramps.description: Start where drawings, tolerances, and handoffs meet the real thing.

choices.title: The drawing was precise. The build still drifted.
choices.scene: Every dimension was present, but the drawing did not carry the installation order, site condition, or tolerance that made those dimensions usable.
choices.lesson: A representation succeeds by preserving the structure needed for an operation—not by containing the whole thing it represents.
choices.structuralMove: Name what the drawing preserves, what it intentionally discards, and which lost feature became consequential during construction.
choices.metaphorFirewall: A blueprint is not the built object, and projection is not automatically error. Disciplined loss is often what makes action possible.
choices.formalBridge: Declare the source, the representation, the intended operation, and the invariant that must survive the projection.

choices.title: Each trade finished its part. The junction failed.
choices.scene: The components met their own specifications. Their shared edge had no single owner, test, or repair path.
choices.conceptLabel: The handoff as a governed boundary
choices.lesson: Local completion does not compose automatically into system completion. The seam needs its own conditions and accountable steward.
choices.structuralMove: Treat the junction as an object: give it an owner, an invariant, an acceptance test, and a route back to repair.
choices.metaphorFirewall: The seam metaphor helps locate responsibility; it does not imply that every failure belongs to exactly one boundary or person.
choices.formalBridge: Model the adjoining parts and their shared interface separately, then test whether their local closure conditions compose.

onramps.label: Research & science
onramps.prompt: The evidence was clear. Its meaning was not.
onramps.description: Start where observation becomes interpretation and claim.

choices.title: A different instrument produced a different answer.
choices.scene: The object remained in place. The unit, resolution, and available comparison changed—and so did the representation.
choices.lesson: Measurement is disciplined access through a declared gauge. An instrument makes some properties comparable while leaving others outside its view.
choices.structuralMove: Separate the object, instrument, measurement conditions, and the property claimed to remain stable across repeated observations.
choices.metaphorFirewall: A ruler is a teaching handle for gauge and disciplined loss; it is not equivalent to every formal use of gauge in mathematics or physics.
choices.formalBridge: Write the representation as a function of the observational gauge, then state which comparison you expect to remain invariant.

choices.title: The result contradicted the model you trusted.
choices.scene: The temptation was to smooth away the outlier. Instead, you preserved the trace and asked where the correspondence first broke.
choices.lesson: A contradiction is not merely an obstacle to publication. Preserved with its conditions, it can localize a defect in model, method, or boundary.
choices.structuralMove: Keep observation and expectation distinct, retain the full trace, and find the earliest comparison that fails.
choices.metaphorFirewall: Not every disagreement falsifies a theory; instrumentation, sampling, transport, and interpretation can also be defective.
choices.formalBridge: Represent expected and observed states separately, then type each possible defect location before choosing a repair.

onramps.label: Policy & institutions
onramps.prompt: The rule worked. Repair did not.
onramps.description: Start where authority blocks challenge, correction, or repair.

choices.title: There was a decision, but no reachable appeal.
choices.scene: The procedure looked complete from inside the institution. From the affected person’s position, the route to challenge an error did not exist.
choices.lesson: A right that cannot be reached, invoked, or completed may be present in text while absent from the person’s actual action-space.
choices.structuralMove: Trace the path from consequence to notice, standing, evidence, review authority, decision, and effective remedy.
choices.metaphorFirewall: The path model reveals reachability; it does not by itself decide what a just outcome must be.
choices.formalBridge: Model agency as the set of actions actually reachable under the institution’s rules, resources, and time constraints.

choices.title: Authority crossed the boundary that justified it.
choices.scene: A role created for one bounded purpose accumulated permissions, acted elsewhere, and left no durable account of the transition.
choices.lesson: Legitimate authority is typed by purpose, domain, permitted actions, evidence, and conditions for review or withdrawal.
choices.structuralMove: Separate possession of capability from authorization to use it, then inspect the transition that enlarged the role.
choices.metaphorFirewall: Boundary language can clarify authority without pretending that institutional legitimacy is a purely technical type-checking problem.
choices.formalBridge: Declare the actor, operating domain, admissible action set, required evidence, and independent closure gate.

onramps.label: Physics & mathematics
onramps.prompt: Something changed. Something had to remain.
onramps.description: Start with change, invariance, scale, and lawful comparison.

choices.title: The form changed, but a relation survived.
choices.scene: Coordinates, notation, or viewpoint shifted. A structure remained stable enough to identify the same object or law across the transformation.
choices.lesson: An invariant states what a permitted transformation must preserve. It gives comparison a lawful spine.
choices.structuralMove: Name the carrier, transformation family, preserved structure, and the conditions that make the transformation admissible.
choices.metaphorFirewall: Finding a pattern that stays visually similar is not enough; formal invariance requires an explicit transformation and preservation law.
choices.formalBridge: Define a transformation on a typed space and test the candidate invariant under every admitted operation.

choices.title: A feature vanished when the scale changed.
choices.scene: The object did not disappear. Under the new resolution, its edge, interior, or local variation no longer survived the projection.
choices.lesson: What exists and what a representation can expose are different questions. Relevant structure can be lost without becoming unreal.
choices.structuralMove: Compare the representations at both scales and identify which feature ceased to be observable—and why that loss matters for the operation.
choices.metaphorFirewall: The example concerns observational regimes; it does not settle ontology or make every defect merely subjective.
choices.formalBridge: Index the representation by resolution, then state the threshold at which the feature required by the task is no longer preserved.

onramps.label: Learning & exploration
onramps.prompt: You need an example before the theory.
onramps.description: Start with a map or metaphor, then follow it into the formal idea.

choices.title: Two maps disagreed and both were useful.
choices.scene: One preserved roads, another weather, another transit connectivity. Each discarded structure the others needed.
choices.conceptLabel: The map is not the territory—but it is not nothing
choices.lesson: A representation is judged by the invariant it preserves for a declared purpose. Incomplete does not mean arbitrary; useful does not mean total.
choices.structuralMove: Ask what operation the map serves, which structure it preserves, and what would break if it were used for a different task.
choices.metaphorFirewall: The map analogy does not imply that truth is relative. A map can be purpose-fit, incomplete, or simply wrong.
choices.formalBridge: Treat the map as a projection from a richer carrier and declare both the preserved invariant and the intentionally lost information.

choices.title: The example became more convincing than the claim.
choices.scene: A familiar story made the structure easy to grasp, then quietly began doing work that only definitions, evidence, or proof could support.
choices.lesson: A metaphor can reveal the shape of an operation. It cannot certify that the formal system has the same properties.
choices.structuralMove: Keep the intuitive handle, label its claim ceiling, and mark the exact point where formal definitions must take over.
choices.metaphorFirewall: A metaphor is a door, not the room.
choices.formalBridge: Translate the example into a declared carrier, boundary, operation, invariant, defect condition, and transport rule.
